# Review of the QuietCart Pilot

QuietCart was a fictional grocery-pickup trial operated by an invented store named Brindle Market. All people and organizations mentioned in this review are fictional. The concept was straightforward: customers selected a ten-minute collection window, and staff carried a prepared order to a numbered bay.

The pilot started with a single primary objective. The store aimed to ease congestion at the service desk on Friday evening. Before launch, the team established a specific metric: at least ⟦T1⟧ of orders were to arrive at the bay within five minutes after the customer’s arrival. They also agreed to check substitutions and missing products as separate issues.

Building the initial version required three weeks. Customers could choose a time slot, provide an order code, and get a brief confirmation. Staff viewed the queue on a tablet. The fictional webpage was ⟦T2⟧, while support used ⟦T3⟧. The synthetic campaign tags were ⟦T4⟧ and ⟦T5⟧-pickup.

On launch night, a substantial queue formed even though the slots appeared evenly distributed. The tablet displayed when customers arrived, but not whether their orders had been packed. For every status update, staff had to contact the stock room. This created repeated calls and caused a minor delay to escalate rapidly.

The team introduced one immediate change. Packers pressed ⟦T6⟧ once a bag reached the shelf. The queue then displayed ready orders in another color. This adjustment allowed runners to see which bay could be served. It did not remove delays in packing, but it prevented staff from looking for orders that were still unfinished.

There were 126 pickups during the first weekend. Seventy-four percent reached the bay within five minutes, which was under the target. Launch night produced a large queue even though every slot looked balanced. The tablet showed arrival time, but it did not show whether an order was packed. Staff had to ask the stock room for each status. That problem created repeated calls and made a small delay grow quickly.

The team made one quick revision. Packers pressed ⟦T6⟧ when a bag reached the shelf. The queue then used a different color for ready orders. This edit helped runners identify which bay they could serve. It did not eliminate late packing, yet it stopped staff from searching for orders that were not ready.

The first weekend had 126 pickups. Seventy-four percent reached the bay within five minutes, below the target. Ready orders met the target frequently; unfinished orders mostly did not. The primary cause was packing capacity between five and six, although three customers also arrived in the wrong slot.

On the second weekend, the shop reduced available slots during the busy hour. That choice could lower total sales, so the team treated it as a trial rather than an obvious fix. Bay delivery rose to ⟦T7⟧ within five minutes. The result met the service target, while total pickup orders stayed similar to the first weekend.

The team used a precise counting method. A runner would check the tablet time against the bay clock and use the same timing rule for every order. Two supervisors reviewed a ten-order sample. Their matching result suggested that the clock rule was correct and sufficient for the pilot, although a larger sample could still expose mistakes.

Customer comments exposed another issue. The confirmation said ⟦T8⟧ but cyclists did not know where to stand. The team added a plain sentence and a shelter marker. This was a little copy edit with a significant effect: staff received fewer location questions, and cyclists had a safer waiting point.

The pilot cost ⟦T9⟧ in temporary signs, devices, and overtime. The shop did not count normal packing wages as a new cost. That boundary is important because including every existing wage would leave the comparison misleading. The retrospective reports the chosen boundary so another reader can reach a different answer.

Two mistakes remained. The team did not retain the initial version of the queue screen, which made later comparison hard. It also changed slot capacity and customer wording during one week. A more controlled test would alter one variable at a time or record why simultaneous action was required.

Staff feedback gave the next clear task. Runners wanted the queue to show shelf location beside the bay number. That edit could reduce walking, but it might increase screen clutter. The team chose to use a paper mockup first. Its goal was to reach a direct answer before another software revision.

QuietCart continued for a six-week extension. The shop chose to keep the ready marker, complete the cyclist shelter, and delete an unused vehicle-description field. The next question was whether the narrower peak schedule would lead to more abandoned orders. The launch offered an encouraging outcome, not a final proof of demand.
